tldr: Tadej Pogačar (UAE Team Emirates - XRG) won the Monaco opener and blew the race apart with a 50 km solo raid in Andorra before a heavy crash on stage 8 ended his Vuelta with a broken collarbone. Enric Mas (Movistar) inherited the red jersey, defended it through three summit finishes and a queen-stage scare from Felix Gall, and completed the biggest win of his career in Granada — the first Spanish overall winner since Alberto Contador in 2014, 2:15 ahead of Primož Roglič and 2:44 ahead of Gall. Sepp Kuss produced the race's other big story on stage 20, riding into a breakaway to leap from 11th to fifth overall, while Tobias Halland Johannessen won a three-up sprint on the closing Granada circuit for his first Grand Tour stage victory. Team Visma \| Lease a Bike topped the stage-win count with seven, five of them from debutant Matthew Brennan.

narrative.headline: Mas completes his Vuelta coronation as Kuss's queen-stage raid and Johannessen's Granada sprint close out the race
narrative.openingMoves: The 2026 Vuelta a España began in Monaco with a short, technical 9.4 km individual time trial that Tadej Pogačar won by nine hundredths of a second over Ethan Hayter, taking the race's first red jersey. Grand Tour debutant Matthew Brennan won the uphill sprint in Manosque on stage 2 after Wout van Aert's late attack for the jersey was caught, and the first summit finish at Font-Romeu on stage 3 was cancelled mid-stage when a hailstorm hit the Col de Mont-Louis, with no winner declared.
narrative.raceUnfolds:
Stage 4 in Andorra was the race-defining day of the first week: Pogačar attacked alone on the Collada de Beixalis with 50 km to go, rode solo over the Coll d'Ordino and won by 2:39, opening a 3:21 overall lead on Primož Roglič. Brennan took a second sprint win on a windy Catalan stage 5, then Pogačar attacked on the gravel of the Puerto de Bartolo on stage 6, was caught by Enric Mas before the summit and beat him in a two-up sprint in Castelló for a third stage win. Andreas Leknessund led a Uno-X one-two at Aramón Valdelinares on stage 7 while Van Aert took the green jersey and Pogačar counter-attacked the GC group to stretch his lead over Mas to 3:50.

Stage 8 to Xeraco changed everything. Roughly 32 km from the finish, on the approach to the Puerto de Barx, Pogačar went down hard in a peloton crash that also caught Ben Tulett. He tried to remount but could not continue and left the race by ambulance with a concussion, a displaced collarbone fracture and a stable neck fracture, the first Grand Tour abandon of his career. Bryan Coquard out-sprinted Mads Pedersen for the stage, and Mas became race leader for the first time in his career, 1:00 ahead of Roglič and 1:11 ahead of Felix Gall.

Mas answered the pressure immediately, attacking inside the final 3 km of the Alto de Aitana queen stage on stage 9 to win and extend his lead to 1:18, with only Oscar Onley able to follow. After the rest day, Bastien Tronchon surprised the sprinters in Elche de la Sierra and Brennan completed a hat-trick in Lorca off a Van Aert lead-out, while Pedersen left the race with illness. On stage 12 Jakob Omrzel soloed to a breakthrough win on Calar Alto as Mas dropped Roglič and Gall on the final climb to push his lead to 1:45; Onley crashed early and slipped to fifth. Van Aert finally took his own stage on stage 13 into Loja, out-sprinting Valentin Paret-Peintre from a two-man move after Brennan neutralised the breakaway's attacks.

Marco Brenner produced a late counter-attack to beat KOM leader Santiago Buitrago atop the Sierra de la Pandera on stage 14 for his first Grand Tour win, while behind them Richard Carapaz lit the fuse on the GC group with an attack that only Mas and Gall could follow; Roglič was distanced in the finale, conceding 25 seconds and second place overall to Gall. Extreme heat forced organisers to cut stage 15 from 189.7 km to 110.2 km, and a five-rider breakaway containing Van Aert, Thibau Nys, Alessandro Romele, Ramses Debruyne and Andreas Leknessund stayed clear to Córdoba, where Van Aert won the sprint for his third stage win; the GC group rolled in together, 2:44 down, with every top-ten position unchanged.

The sprinters finally got two clean shots at the finish after that run of climbing and breakaway days. On stage 16 to La Rábida a five-man break built a lead of nearly three minutes before Team Visma | Lease a Bike reeled it in with about 24 km to go; a coastal crosswind briefly split the peloton, but Van Aert delivered Brennan to his fourth stage win. Stage 17, the flattest of the race, into Sevilla followed the same script — an early trio built a five-minute gap before being caught inside the final 3 km, and Van Aert again set up Brennan, who came around Magnus Cort to win clear for a fifth stage win. Both bunch sprints left the general classification untouched.

The race resumed its GC business on stage 18, a 32.1 km time trial from El Puerto de Santa María to Jerez de la Frontera. Stefan Küng won the stage by three seconds over Callum Thornley, but the story was behind them: Roglič went out hard, opening 36 seconds on Mas by the second checkpoint, and although Mas clawed some back over the technical closing kilometres he still conceded 33 seconds overall. That was enough for Roglič to leapfrog Felix Gall, who lost 1:28 on the flat course, back into second overall. Stage 19 to Peñas Blancas brought the Costa del Sol's Cat-1 summit finish, and it was the day's 16-rider breakaway that decided the stage — Santiago Buitrago attacked inside the final 2.5 km, only for Eddie Dunbar to run him down and pass him within the last 500 m for his third career Vuelta stage win. Behind, Red Bull-BORA-hansgrohe and then Movistar and EF Education-EasyPost set the pace on the closing climb, and when Roglič tested the group with a late attack, Mas responded immediately alongside Gall, Onley and Carapaz; the five finished together, 5:11 down on Dunbar. Mattias Skjelmose was the only GC rider distanced, losing 1:15 and slipping from eighth to ninth overall.

Stage 20, the queen stage to the Collado del Alguacil, produced the race's last twist. A 54-rider move including Mikel Landa, Ramses Debruyne and Tobias Halland Johannessen formed the day's main breakaway, and Sepp Kuss and Richard Carapaz launched the first GC counter-attack of the day on the Puerto de El Purche, with Mas, Roglič and Gall bridging up behind them. Landa, Debruyne and Johannessen split clear of the rest of the break on the run-in to the final climb, and Landa attacked alone early on the Alguacil to solo to his first Grand Tour stage win in five years, 47 seconds clear of Johannessen. Behind, Gall attacked out of the Mas-Roglič-Carapaz group partway up the climb; Mas responded but let him go, and Roglič was also dropped before stabilising the gap, leaving the GC podium order unchanged but with Gall clawing back a little time. The stage's biggest story was further back: Kuss, who had bridged into the early counter-move, rode all the way to the finish to leap from 11th overall into fifth, jumping Onley, Omrzel, Berthet, Rodríguez, Skjelmose and Tejada in one move and effectively deciding the final GC order below the podium.
narrative.decision: Decided on stage 20's Collado del Alguacil summit finish: Enric Mas held off Felix Gall's late attack to protect his lead, extending his overall advantage to 2:15 over Primož Roglič and 2:44 over Gall — a margin that carried unchanged through the largely processional stage 21 into Granada. Richard Carapaz finished fourth overall at 6:54, with Sepp Kuss's stage-20 breakaway gambit securing him fifth at 8:45, ahead of Oscar Onley (+9:28), Jakob Omrzel (+10:38), Clément Berthet (+11:41), Cristián Rodríguez (+11:59) and Harold Tejada (+12:51) rounding out the top ten.
narrative.finale: Stage 21 broke from the traditional Madrid procession, finishing in Granada for the first time in the race's 81 editions. Movistar controlled a ceremonial opening before the route reached a Granada circuit with a repeated 2.2 km climb to the Alhambra, which shattered the peloton and produced a genuinely attacking finale even though the GC times were frozen with 9.8 km to go, officially confirming Mas as champion. Tobias Halland Johannessen emerged from the winning move to beat Alessandro Romele and Ramses Debruyne in a three-up sprint for his first Grand Tour stage win, with Matthew Brennan leading the chase group home fourth. Mas dropped back through the field to cross the line with his Movistar teammates, completing the biggest victory of his career and ending Spain's 12-year wait for a home Vuelta winner since Alberto Contador in 2014.

decisiveMoments.headline: Pogačar wins the opening time trial by 0.09 seconds
decisiveMoments.description: On a technical, corner-heavy 9.4 km course through Monaco, Tadej Pogačar started second-to-last and edged out Ethan Hayter by nine hundredths of a second to take the stage and the race's first red jersey.

decisiveMoments.headline: Pogačar's 50 km solo raid blows the GC apart
decisiveMoments.description: Pogačar attacked on gradients of up to 16 percent with 50 km to go, rode alone over the Coll d'Ordino and won by 2:39 on the chasing group, turning a nine-second lead into a 3:21 advantage over Roglič after just four stages.

decisiveMoments.location: Approach to the Puerto de Barx (Stage 8)
decisiveMoments.headline: The race leader crashes out
decisiveMoments.description: A heavy peloton crash roughly 32 km from the finish in Xeraco left Pogačar with a concussion and a broken collarbone. He tried to remount but was withdrawn by ambulance, handing the red jersey to Enric Mas and resetting a race Pogačar had led by 3:50.

decisiveMoments.headline: Mas wins the queen stage in his first day in red
decisiveMoments.description: Rather than defend, Enric Mas attacked inside the final 3 km of the week-one queen stage, dropped every rival except Oscar Onley and took the stage to extend his lead to 1:18 over Roglič.

decisiveMoments.headline: Mas drops Roglič and Gall to push his lead past 1:45
decisiveMoments.description: On the final ramps of Calar Alto, Mas accelerated away from Roglič and Gall while Jakob Omrzel won the stage from the break, stretching the overall lead to 1:45 with the Sierra de la Pandera and Sierra Nevada still ahead.

decisiveMoments.headline: Carapaz's attack costs Roglič second overall
decisiveMoments.description: Richard Carapaz attacked the GC group low on the final climb; only Mas and Gall could go with him, and Roglič, closing the gap late, was repeatedly caught out in the finale and dropped. He conceded 25 seconds and second place overall to Gall, who now sits at 2:06 with Roglič third at 2:10.

decisiveMoments.location: Jerez de la Frontera time trial (Stage 18)
decisiveMoments.headline: Roglič retakes second overall in the time trial
decisiveMoments.description: Primož Roglič opened 36 seconds on Enric Mas by the second time check of the 32.1 km test and, despite Mas pulling some back over the closing kilometres, still took 33 seconds out of the race leader. Felix Gall lost 1:28 on the flat course, dropping him back to third overall as Roglič retook second at 1:37 behind Mas.

decisiveMoments.headline: Roglič probes, Mas responds, Skjelmose is the only casualty
decisiveMoments.description: On the closing Cat-1 climb to Peñas Blancas, Roglič attacked inside the final kilometre to test the red jersey, but Mas covered the move immediately with Gall, Onley and Carapaz also holding the wheel. Mattias Skjelmose was the lone GC rider distanced, losing 1:15 and dropping from eighth to ninth overall, while the stage itself went to the breakaway's Eddie Dunbar.

decisiveMoments.headline: Gall's late attack narrows the gap without changing the podium
decisiveMoments.description: Felix Gall attacked out of the Mas-Roglič-Carapaz group partway up the queen stage's final climb. Mas responded initially but let him go, and Roglič was also dropped before stabilising the gap; Gall clawed back a little time on both but the final podium order held — Mas 2:15 clear of Roglič, with Gall a further 29 seconds back.

decisiveMoments.headline: Kuss's breakaway gambit vaults him from 11th to fifth overall
decisiveMoments.description: Sepp Kuss bridged into the day's early GC counter-attack alongside Richard Carapaz and rode through to the finish, leaping from 11th overall into fifth — jumping Oscar Onley, Jakob Omrzel, Clément Berthet, Cristián Rodríguez, Mattias Skjelmose and Harold Tejada in a single move that decided the final GC order below the podium.

decisiveMoments.headline: GC frozen before the final lap, confirming Mas as champion
decisiveMoments.description: With the front group beginning the final lap of the Alhambra circuit 9.8 km from the finish, race officials fixed the general classification times, officially securing Enric Mas's overall victory before the sprint for the stage was even decided.

riderPerformances.name: Tadej Pogačar
riderPerformances.narrative: Pogačar won the Monaco time trial, the 50 km Andorra raid on stage 4 and the gravel finale in Castelló on stage 6, and had stretched his overall lead to 3:50 by stage 7 in what was shaping up as a crushing first Vuelta victory. A heavy peloton crash on the flat run-in to Xeraco on stage 8 ended it: a concussion, a displaced collarbone fracture and a stable neck fracture forced the first Grand Tour abandon of his career. He had collarbone surgery on 31 August.

keyMoments.what: Stage 1: won the Monaco ITT by 0.09 seconds to take the race lead
Stage 4: 50 km solo attack from the Collada de Beixalis; won by 2:39 and opened a 3:21 GC lead
Stage 6: attacked on the Puerto de Bartolo gravel and beat Enric Mas in a two-up sprint for his third stage win
Stage 8: crashed heavily approaching the Puerto de Barx and abandoned with a broken collarbone

incident.detail: Stage 8: heavy peloton crash ~32 km from the finish; concussion, displaced left clavicle fracture and stable C7 fracture forced his withdrawal

riderPerformances.name: Felix Gall
riderPerformances.narrative: Gall was the only rider able to follow Pogačar's first acceleration on the Beixalis and was the most aggressive of the remaining contenders throughout the second half of the race, attacking repeatedly on Valdelinares and Aitana before matching Carapaz's decisive move on the Sierra de la Pandera to rise to second overall. The 32.1 km Jerez time trial on stage 18 cost him the runner-up spot to Roglič, dropping him back to third at 3:01. On the closing Collado del Alguacil queen stage he launched the day's most dangerous GC attack, distancing Mas and Roglič to claw back time on both, and completed the race on the final podium, 2:44 behind Mas and 29 seconds ahead of Roglič's gap to him.

keyMoments.what: Stage 9: repeated attacks on Aitana moved him to third overall
Stage 12: dropped by Mas alongside Roglič on Calar Alto
Stage 14: matches Carapaz's attack and Mas's pace on Pandera to move up to second overall
Stage 18: concedes 1:28 to Roglič in the Jerez time trial, drops back to third overall
Stage 20: attacks the GC group on the Collado del Alguacil, claws back time on Mas and Roglič to secure third overall

riderPerformances.name: Primož Roglič
riderPerformances.narrative: Roglič conceded 22 seconds in the Monaco opener and 2:39 to Pogačar's Andorra raid, and was distanced again on the Bartolo gravel and at Valdelinares. Pogačar's abandon lifted him to second overall, and Enric Mas dropped him twice more, on Aitana and Calar Alto, before he lost the runner-up spot itself on stage 14, conceding it to Gall. He answered on stage 18, riding the most aggressive time trial of the GC contenders to take 33 seconds out of Mas and retake second overall at 1:37, then tested the red jersey with a late attack on Peñas Blancas on stage 19 that Mas covered immediately. On the closing queen stage to the Collado del Alguacil he bridged to an early GC counter-move but was dropped by Gall's decisive attack on the final climb, stabilising the gap to complete the race second overall, 2:15 behind Mas.

keyMoments.what: Stage 9: third on Aitana, 12 seconds behind Mas, holding second overall
Stage 12: dropped by Mas on the final climb of Calar Alto; gap grows to 1:45
Stage 14: dropped in the finale of Pandera, conceding second overall to Gall
Stage 18: takes 33 seconds out of Mas in the time trial to retake second overall
Stage 19: attacks inside the final kilometre of Peñas Blancas; Mas responds immediately
Stage 20: dropped by Gall's attack on the Collado del Alguacil, stabilises the gap to finish second overall

riderPerformances.name: Richard Carapaz
riderPerformances.narrative: Carapaz led the chase over the Beixalis behind Pogačar but lost ground at Valdelinares, then bounced back on Aitana by attacking across to the breakaway remnants. On stage 14 he lit the fuse on the GC battle himself, attacking low on the Sierra de la Pandera with only Mas and Gall able to follow all the way. He held fourth overall through the flat stages and the Jerez time trial, and combined with Sepp Kuss to launch the day's first GC counter-attack on the Collado del Alguacil in the final week, though he could not follow the later moves from Gall on the summit finish itself. He completed the race fourth overall at 6:54.

keyMoments.what: Stage 9: attacked from the GC group across to the break on Aitana
Stage 14: launches the attack on Pandera that splits the GC group
Stage 20: combines with Kuss to launch the first GC counter-attack on the Puerto de El Purche

riderPerformances.name: Oscar Onley
riderPerformances.narrative: Onley followed the key moves on Beixalis and was the only rider to stay with Mas on the Alto de Aitana, finishing second on the queen stage and rising to fourth overall. An early crash on stage 12 compromised his day on Calar Alto and he slipped to fifth, then lost the position again when Sepp Kuss's long-range breakaway move on the Collado del Alguacil pushed him down to sixth overall. He completed the race there, 9:28 behind Mas, while securing the best young rider's white jersey.

keyMoments.what: Stage 9: second on Aitana, the only rider to follow Mas
Stage 12: slid out on a roundabout, chased back, lost time on Calar Alto
Stage 14: dropped from the Mas-Gall-Roglič-Carapaz group in the closing kilometres of Pandera
Stage 20: passed by Kuss's breakaway move on the Collado del Alguacil, drops to sixth overall

incident.detail: Stage 12: slid out on a roundabout ~131 km from the finish; remounted and rejoined the peloton

riderPerformances.name: Mattias Skjelmose
riderPerformances.narrative: Skjelmose lost contact with the favourites on the closing climb in Andorra and shed more time on the Bartolo gravel and at Valdelinares, but turned to the breakaway for GC gains, clawing back roughly two minutes in the stage 13 break into Loja. He was dropped again on the Sierra de la Pandera on stage 14 and lost a further 1:15 on Peñas Blancas on stage 19, dropping to ninth overall. The third week's accumulated fatigue caught up with him on the Collado del Alguacil queen stage, where he shipped significant time as fresher rivals moved past him in the standings, and he finished the race 13th overall at 25:43, well outside the top ten he had held for most of the final week.

keyMoments.what: Stage 13: rode the day-long breakaway to gain around two minutes on the GC group
Stage 14: dropped from the GC group on the final climb of Pandera
Stage 19: distanced from the group of GC favourites on the closing climb to Peñas Blancas
Stage 20: loses significant time on the Collado del Alguacil as third-week fatigue takes hold, slipping out of the top ten

riderPerformances.name: Matthew Brennan
riderPerformances.narrative: The 21-year-old Grand Tour debutant won five stages: the uphill sprint in Manosque on stage 2, a led-out sprint on stage 5, the reduced-bunch finish in Lorca on stage 11, and back-to-back bunch sprints in La Rábida on stage 16 and Sevilla on stage 17, all but stage 11 set up by a Wout van Aert lead-out. On stage 13 he returned the favour, riding in the break and shutting down every attack so Van Aert could win. In Granada on the final stage he was briefly distanced on the Alhambra climb during Pello Bilbao's attack but fought back to the front group, only to be left without a lead-out as Johannessen, Romele and Debruyne slipped clear inside the final two kilometres; he led the chasing group home fourth to close out the most successful Grand Tour debut of the 2026 season.

keyMoments.what: Stage 2: won the uphill sprint in Manosque for his first Grand Tour stage win
Stage 5: second stage win from a Visma lead-out
Stage 11: hat-trick in Lorca off Van Aert's lead-out
Stage 13: neutralised the break so Van Aert could win
Stage 16: fourth stage win in La Rábida off another Van Aert lead-out
Stage 17: fifth stage win in Sevilla, coming around Magnus Cort
Stage 21: left without support as the winning trio goes clear, leads the chase group home fourth

riderPerformances.name: Wout van Aert
riderPerformances.narrative: Van Aert attacked for the jersey on stage 2, took the green jersey with a day-long attack to third at Valdelinares on stage 7, and led out most of Brennan's sprint wins. On stage 13 he won his own Vuelta stage for the first time, out-sprinting Valentin Paret-Peintre in Loja from a two-man move, then made it two in a row on the heat-shortened stage 15 into Córdoba, winning a five-up sprint from the day's decisive breakaway. He guided Brennan to a fourth win in La Rábida on stage 16 and a fifth in Sevilla on stage 17, and closed out the queen stage on stage 20 by winning the KOM sprint atop the Puerto de El Purche twice before pacing Sepp Kuss through the GC group, ending his own mountains-jersey bid to help set up Kuss's leap to fifth overall. On the Granada finale he was dropped when Pello Bilbao attacked on the Alhambra climb. He completed the race with the points classification won comfortably ahead of teammate Brennan.

keyMoments.what: Stage 2: attacked inside the final kilometre in a bid for the race lead
Stage 7: third from the day-long break; took the green jersey
Stage 13: first Vuelta stage win, beating Paret-Peintre in Loja
Stage 15: wins a five-up sprint in Córdoba from the day's decisive breakaway
Stage 16: delivers Brennan to his fourth stage win in a headwind lead-out
Stage 17: guides Brennan onto Magnus Cort's wheel for a fifth stage win
Stage 20: wins the KOM sprint atop the Puerto de El Purche for the second time, then paces Kuss through the GC group
Stage 21: dropped by Bilbao's attack on the Alhambra climb

riderPerformances.name: Pello Bilbao
riderPerformances.narrative: Riding his final Grand Tour, Bilbao was honoured in the pre-stage ceremony on the road into Granada before attacking on the Alhambra climb with 9km remaining, dropping Van Aert and Bryan Coquard and opening a useful gap before Axel Laurance caught and passed him. He was brought back with the rest of the group inside the final 5km and finished sixth on the day, a memorable send-off attack to close out his career.

keyMoments.what: Stage 21: attacks on the Alhambra climb, drops Van Aert and Coquard

riderPerformances.name: Jordi Meeus
riderPerformances.narrative: Meeus was among the first sprinters distanced as the repeated ascents of the Alhambra circuit whittled the peloton down on the final stage, playing no part in the finale.

crashes.location: Stage 8, approach to the Puerto de Barx
crashes.description: Heavy peloton crash roughly 32 km from the finish at Xeraco, also involving Ben Tulett. Pogačar hit the tarmac hard, suffering a concussion, a displaced left collarbone fracture and a stable C7 vertebra fracture; he underwent collarbone surgery on 31 August.
Onley slid out on a roundabout about 131 km from the finish, remounted and chased back to the bunch, then lost further time on Calar Alto and dropped from fourth to fifth overall.

abandons.reason: Withdrawn by ambulance on stage 8 after a heavy crash with a suspected broken collarbone and a head injury while leading the race by 3:50 — the first Grand Tour abandon of his career.
Did not start stage 11 after withdrawing with illness.

aftermath.headline: Enric Mas wins the 2026 Vuelta a España, ending Spain's 12-year wait for a home champion
aftermath.body: Enric Mas (Movistar) completed the 2026 Vuelta a España as the overall winner in Granada, 2:15 ahead of Primož Roglič and 2:44 ahead of Felix Gall, converting three previous Vuelta runner-up finishes into his first Grand Tour title and becoming the first Spanish winner of the race since Alberto Contador in 2014. Mas inherited the red jersey after Tadej Pogačar's race-ending crash on stage 8 — Pogačar had led by 3:50 with three stage wins before the heavy fall that fractured his collarbone and forced surgery — and defended it through summit finishes at Aitana, Calar Alto and Peñas Blancas, a 32.1 km time trial, and a late attack from Gall on the closing Collado del Alguacil queen stage. That same stage produced the race's other headline story, as Sepp Kuss rode into the day's decisive breakaway to leap from 11th to fifth overall, reshuffling the bottom half of the final top ten. The Granada finale, held for the first time in the race's history, was a processional coronation for Mas but a genuinely attacking day for the stage: Tobias Halland Johannessen beat Alessandro Romele and Ramses Debruyne in a three-up sprint on the repeated Alhambra circuit for his first Grand Tour stage win, with Matthew Brennan — the race's most successful sprinter with five stage wins in his Grand Tour debut — leading the chase group home fourth. Wout van Aert won the points classification, Santiago Buitrago the mountains classification, and Oscar Onley the best young rider's white jersey.
